transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I’m here because I’ve been feeling like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. At work, especially. I’m a physician, and people come in assuming I’m competent and safe and worthy of making decisions for them, and lately I keep getting stuck on these small things—little clinical imperfections, things that objectively might be minor, or that other people would probably just learn from and move on from—and I replay them over and over.

It starts to feel like they’re not just mistakes or near-mistakes, but proof of something bigger, like proof that I’m dangerous, that I shouldn’t be allowed to have that level of responsibility. I know that sounds… dramatic, maybe, but it feels very real when I’m in it. Like every small imperfection confirms that I’ve been fooling everyone who trusts me.
Do you find yourself unable to stop thinking about these imperfections even when you try to focus on other things?

Yes. Very much so. I try to set it aside, especially because in medicine you’re supposed to be able to review something, learn from it, maybe discuss it if needed, and then keep functioning. But I’ll get stuck on these tiny clinical imperfections—like something I said slightly unclearly, or a decision point where maybe there was a better option—and it doesn’t stay proportional.

It becomes this loop where I keep replaying it, almost like I’m trying to find the exact moment that proves I shouldn’t be trusted. And even if part of me can recognize that other physicians make small mistakes or have cases they’d handle differently in hindsight, when it’s me, it feels like evidence that I’m dangerous. Like patients and colleagues are putting trust in me that I haven’t earned, or that I’ve somehow deceived them into thinking I’m safe.

So yes, even when I’m trying to focus on other things, it keeps coming back. It’s not just, “I could improve that.” It’s more like, “This proves something is wrong with me as a doctor.”
Do you experience these intrusive thoughts or feelings of inadequacy in areas of your life outside of your work as a physician?

Mostly it’s centered on work… or at least that’s where it becomes the most intense and concrete. I think because being a physician means people are literally trusting me with things that matter, and when I notice some small imperfection, even something that might not be a major error, I don’t experience it as small. I replay it like it’s evidence that I’m not deserving of that trust.

Outside of work, I guess the same feeling can kind of color how I see myself, but I don’t have as clear an example. It’s not like I’m making a mistake doing something ordinary and spiraling in exactly the same way. The physician part is where it really attaches. Patients, colleagues, the whole system sort of assuming I’m competent and safe… and then I feel like I’m secretly not, like I’ve been allowed into a role I shouldn’t have.

So, yes and no. The inadequacy feels like it’s about me as a person, but the thoughts that really get intrusive are mostly around clinical situations—small imperfections that start to feel like proof that I’m dangerous as a doctor.
Are these thoughts and feelings of inadequacy affecting your relationships with family or friends outside of work?

Yes… I think it is, though maybe not in a dramatic way where there’s been some big conflict or anything. It’s more like I’ve become less available, less reliable socially. I still show up to clinic, I’m still doing the core parts of my job, but it takes so much out of me to get through that and to keep checking myself that by the time I’m outside of work, I don’t really trust that I have good judgment or enough energy to be present with people.

So if friends ask me to make plans, I’ll often avoid committing, or I’ll cancel, or I’ll say I’m too busy when really I just don’t feel capable of being normal company. And with family, I’m not exactly arguing with them, but I’m more withdrawn. I don’t reach out as much. I worry that I’ll say something off or that I won’t be able to respond appropriately, and then it feels easier not to engage.

At work, too, I’ve noticed I’ve had to ask for help with some non-urgent administrative things—not patient care in the moment, but paperwork or follow-up tasks that I would usually just handle—because I get bogged down and second-guess myself. So… yes, it’s starting to affect how reliably I function, and outside of work it’s definitely making me less connected to people.
Do you feel like these thoughts and feelings of inadequacy are significantly interfering with your overall quality of life?

Yes… I think it is. I mean, I’m still functioning in the sense that I’m showing up to clinic and doing what I absolutely have to do, so part of me keeps trying to tell myself it can’t be that serious. But it doesn’t feel like my life is normal right now.

It’s like I can get through the workday, but it takes so much effort and second-guessing that I don’t have much left afterward. And even at work, I’ve had to ask for help with non-urgent administrative things—paperwork, follow-up tasks, things I would usually just handle—because I get stuck and can’t move through them efficiently. That feels embarrassing, because these aren’t things that should overwhelm me.

Outside of work, I’m avoiding plans with friends, or not committing in the first place, because I don’t trust my judgment or my energy. I worry I won’t be able to be present, or I’ll say the wrong thing, or I’ll just be this drained, preoccupied version of myself. So I end up isolating more, and then I feel even less connected.

So yes, it’s interfering. Maybe not in a completely catastrophic way, but enough that I don’t feel reliable in the way I used to—at work or with people in my life.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings of inadequacy and intrusive thoughts?

It’s been… a little over a year, I think. About a year and a month now.

It started after I received this clinic award, which is strange, because outwardly that should have felt reassuring or validating. People were being kind, and it was supposed to mean I was doing well. But for me it almost had the opposite effect. After that, I started feeling like the gap between how people saw me and how I saw myself was unbearable. Like the award made it more visible that people believed I was competent, and then I became much more preoccupied with the idea that I didn’t actually deserve that.

So, yes—roughly thirteen months. It wasn’t just a bad week or a short stressful period. It’s been persistent since then, with the intrusive thoughts and inadequacy kind of building around that time.
Do you feel like these thoughts and feelings of inadequacy are causing you a lot of emotional pain or distress?

Yes… it is. It’s probably the main reason I’m here, honestly. It’s not just that I feel a bit insecure or that I’m having normal self-doubt. It feels much more painful than that.

I keep feeling like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. Patients, colleagues, staff—people treat me as if I’m competent and safe and responsible, and instead of feeling reassured by that, I feel this… almost unbearable guilt. Like I’m misleading them somehow just by showing up in the role.

And then I replay small clinical imperfections over and over. Not even always major things—sometimes it’s a wording choice, or a moment where I think I could have asked one more question, or I didn’t explain something as smoothly as I should have. I’ll go back through it in my head as if that one moment proves something terrible about me. Like it proves I’m not just imperfect, but dangerous. Like I shouldn’t be trusted.

So yes, it causes a lot of distress. I know on some level that every doctor has imperfect moments, but emotionally it doesn’t land that way. It feels like evidence against me, and I keep returning to it even when I’m trying not to.
Are there specific situations or tasks that you're avoiding because of these intrusive thoughts and feelings of inadequacy?

Yes… there are. I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped doing everything, because I am still going to clinic and seeing patients and doing the things I absolutely have to do. But there are definitely tasks I’m avoiding or putting off, especially the non-urgent administrative stuff.

Like paperwork, follow-up messages, little forms, scheduling-related things, documentation that isn’t immediately critical… things that normally I would just handle between patients or at the end of the day. Lately I get kind of stuck on them. I’ll open something and then start second-guessing the wording, or whether I’m missing some implication, or whether doing it wrong somehow reflects that I’m not reliable. And then it takes far longer than it should, or I just can’t make myself finish it. I’ve had to ask for help with some of those things, which feels humiliating, because objectively they’re not hard tasks.

And socially, I’ve been avoiding plans more than I want to admit. If friends ask to do something after work or on the weekend, I’ll hesitate or give a vague answer, because I don’t trust that I’ll have the energy or that I’ll be normal to be around. I worry I’ll be distracted, or say something off, or just sit there feeling like I’m pretending. So I end up not committing, or I cancel, or I let things fade.

So… yes. I’m still functioning, but in a narrower way. I can do the essential parts, mostly, but the extra pieces of work and the connection with people outside of work have started to slip.
Do you feel compelled to perform specific rituals or behaviors in an attempt to reduce your anxiety or make up for the perceived mistakes you've made as a physician?

I’m not sure I’d call them rituals, exactly. I mean… not in the way I think you might mean, like a fixed sequence I have to do a certain number of times, or something very formalized.

I do find myself going back over things mentally, or checking wording more than I probably need to, especially if I think I may have made a mistake. But it doesn’t feel like a specific ritual that reliably reduces the anxiety. If anything, it often makes me more stuck, because I keep trying to reach some feeling of certainty or reassurance that doesn’t really come.

So… I don’t know. I don’t think I have a particular behavior I do to “make up for” it, at least not one I can identify clearly. It’s more like I get caught in reviewing and second-guessing, but not a defined ritual.
Are you avoiding social interactions or relationships outside of work due to feelings of inadequacy or fear of being judged?

Yes… I think I am. Not completely, like I haven’t cut everyone off or decided I’m never seeing anyone again, but I’m definitely avoiding more than I used to.

If someone asks me to get dinner, or meet up on the weekend, or even just have a normal conversation after work, I find myself hesitating. I start thinking, “What if I’m too drained? What if I can’t follow the conversation properly? What if I seem strange or distracted?” And then underneath that there’s this more embarrassing feeling that I’m not really worth people’s time, or that if they pay close attention they’ll notice I’m not as competent or steady as they think I am.

So I either don’t commit, or I give some vague answer, or I cancel. And each time I tell myself it’s just because I’m tired or busy, which is partly true, but it’s also because I don’t trust my judgment or my energy right now. I don’t trust that I’ll show up in a way that feels normal.

And it’s kind of the same pattern as work, honestly. I’m still showing up to clinic and doing the essential things, but I’ve had to ask for help with some non-urgent administrative tasks because I get stuck or overwhelmed by them. Outside of work, the equivalent is that I’m letting social plans slip. So I’m functioning, but less reliably than before, and I feel less connected to people.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to perform your job as a physician or maintain your relationships since these feelings of inadequacy started?

Yes… I have noticed changes. I’m still going to clinic, and I’m still seeing patients, so from the outside it may look like I’m basically functioning. And I don’t want to overstate it, because I haven’t stopped working or anything like that. But it’s definitely not the same.

The main thing at work is that I can still do the essential, immediate parts of the job, but the less urgent things are where I start to fall apart a bit. Administrative work, messages, forms, documentation that isn’t critical right that second… I find myself getting stuck, second-guessing, taking much longer than I should. And I’ve had to ask for help with some of it, which feels awful, honestly, because those are things I should be able to manage. They’re not complex medical decisions, but I still don’t trust myself to handle them efficiently or correctly.

And outside of work, yes, it’s affected relationships too. I’ve been avoiding social plans, not because I don’t care about people, but because I don’t trust my energy or my judgment. I worry I’ll be too drained, or distracted, or not able to be present. So I hesitate, or don’t commit, or let things fade. Then I feel more disconnected, which makes it harder to reach out the next time.

So… I’m still functioning, but less reliably. It’s like my life has narrowed to the bare minimum: show up for clinic, get through the necessary things, and then avoid anything extra because I’m not sure I can handle it.
Have you had to take any time off work due to the distress caused by these thoughts and feelings of inadequacy?

No… I haven’t actually taken time off work, at least not in the formal sense. I’m still showing up to clinic. That’s part of what makes it feel strange, because if you looked at my schedule you might think, well, he’s working, he’s seeing patients, so he must be managing.

But it does feel like I’m managing by narrowing things down to only what absolutely has to happen. I can get myself there, I can do the clinic day, I can focus on the immediate patient-facing responsibilities. But then the non-urgent administrative pieces… those are the things I start getting stuck on. Messages, forms, tasks that require me to sit down and make decisions without a clear immediate pressure. I’ve had to ask for help with some of that, which is embarrassing for me to admit.

So, no, I haven’t taken sick days or stepped away from work because of it. But I also wouldn’t say work is unaffected. It’s more that I’m still present, but less reliable around the edges. And outside of work I’m avoiding plans more, because by the time I’m done I don’t really trust my energy or my judgment enough to see people or commit to anything. So I’m functioning, but it feels more fragile than it used to.
Have you felt like quitting your job as a physician due to these feelings of inadequacy?

I’ve thought about it in passing, yes… but I don’t think I’m at the point of actually quitting. It’s more like the thought comes up when I’m overwhelmed, like, “Maybe I’m not cut out for this,” or “Maybe everyone would be better off if I stepped away.” But then I still go in. I’m still showing up to clinic, still seeing patients, still doing the parts that absolutely have to get done.

Where it’s showing up more concretely is around the edges of the job. The non-urgent administrative work has become much harder for me to keep up with. Messages, forms, paperwork, things that don’t have an immediate patient sitting in front of me… I get stuck and I overthink them, and I’ve had to ask for help with some of that. That feels humiliating, honestly, because it makes me question whether I’m functioning the way I should be.

So no, I haven’t made plans to quit, and I haven’t stopped working. But I do feel less reliable than I used to, and that scares me. It also spills over outside of work, because by the time I’m done holding it together at clinic, I avoid social plans. I don’t trust that I’ll have the energy or the judgment to be present with people. So it’s not that I’m quitting my job, but my world has definitely gotten smaller.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts about your competence as a physician are completely under your control?

No… I don’t think they feel completely under my control. I can sometimes argue with them intellectually, if that makes sense. Like, part of me knows that every physician has small imperfections, or moments they wish they’d handled more smoothly. I can say that to myself in a rational way.

But then another part of my mind keeps returning to them as if they mean something much bigger. I’ll replay some small clinical interaction or a minor decision or something I documented imperfectly, and it starts to feel like evidence that I shouldn’t be trusted. Not just that I made a mistake, but that I’m fundamentally not safe, or that I don’t deserve the trust patients and colleagues put in me.

That’s actually a big part of why I’m here. It’s not just ordinary self-criticism anymore. It feels intrusive and sticky. I’ll try to move on, and then it comes back with this tone of, “See, this proves you’re dangerous,” even when the actual issue is small or ambiguous. I don’t feel like I can simply decide not to think that way. I can push back for a while, but I don’t feel in full control of it.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts about your competence are a part of your own beliefs, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of yourself?

It feels like… mostly it feels like it’s coming from inside me. Not like a separate voice outside my head or anything like that. It’s my own mind, my own judgment, but it’s become so harsh and so repetitive that it doesn’t feel like ordinary reflection anymore.

I mean, I’m here because I keep having this conviction that I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. Patients trust me, colleagues trust me, and instead of being able to accept that as normal professional responsibility, I keep feeling like I’ve somehow fooled everyone. I’ll replay these small clinical imperfections — a phrase I used, a decision that could have been cleaner, something I documented in a way that wasn’t perfect — and then my mind treats it like proof. Like, “There, that shows you’re dangerous. That shows you shouldn’t be doing this.”

So it feels like my belief, in the sense that I’m the one thinking it and I can’t honestly say it feels external. But it also feels… distorted, or outsized. Like a part of me knows the examples are small, but another part of me attaches this enormous moral weight to them. I don’t experience it as someone else putting the thought into my head. It’s more that my own thoughts have turned against me, if that makes sense.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are in line with your own values and beliefs about yourself?

I think… yes and no. They feel in line with the worst things I believe about myself right now, but not with what I would have said about myself before this started getting so consuming.

I mean, I have always taken being a doctor seriously. I do believe patients’ trust is sacred, and I do believe that small things matter clinically. So in that sense, the thoughts attach themselves to values I really do have — responsibility, caution, not being careless, not harming people. That part is real. I don’t want to be someone who dismisses mistakes or shrugs off imperfections.

But the way my mind is using those values now feels… disproportionate. I’m here because I feel like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. And I keep replaying small clinical imperfections as if they prove I’m a dangerous doctor. Not just “you could improve that,” but “this proves something rotten about you,” or “you shouldn’t be trusted with patients.” That feels more like guilt turning into a verdict, if that makes sense.

So I guess the thoughts are connected to my values, but they’ve become cruel. They don’t feel like balanced professional standards anymore. They feel like my mind taking any tiny imperfection and using it as evidence that I’m fundamentally unworthy of the role.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are something you can agree with, or do they feel alien to you?

I think… they don’t feel completely alien, and that’s part of what makes them so hard to dismiss.

If they felt totally foreign, like some bizarre thought that had nothing to do with me, maybe I could say, “That’s not me, that’s just noise.” But they hook into something I already care about very deeply — being careful, deserving trust, not harming anyone, not taking the role lightly. So when the thought says, “You don’t deserve the trust people put in you,” it doesn’t feel random. It feels like it’s using my own standards against me.

But do I agree with it? I don’t know. Some part of me does, or at least gets pulled into agreeing with it. I’ll replay some small clinical imperfection — something I said, something I could have documented better, a decision that wasn’t perfectly clean in retrospect — and in that moment it feels like evidence. It starts to feel like, “This proves you’re unsafe. This proves you’re a dangerous doctor.” And emotionally, I can end up believing that, even if another part of me knows the conclusion is way too extreme.

So I wouldn’t say it feels alien exactly. It feels like my own guilt and self-judgment, but intensified to the point where it becomes almost impossible to reason with. It feels like a verdict about me rather than a thought I can just evaluate and set aside.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are consistent with the kind of person you think you are?

I think… uncomfortably, yes. Or at least it feels consistent with the kind of person I think I am when I’m at my worst.

I’ve always thought of myself as someone who should be careful, conscientious, maybe even exacting. I don’t think that part is false. I do believe that being trusted as a doctor is a serious thing, and I’ve always felt that if patients are putting themselves in my hands, then I have to be worthy of that. So when these thoughts come up, they don’t feel completely out of character. They feel like an extreme version of something that already matters to me.

But the way it lands now is much harsher. It’s not just, “You’re the kind of person who wants to improve,” or, “You should reflect on what could have gone better.” It becomes, “You don’t deserve the trust people put in you.” And then I’ll take these small clinical imperfections — something I said awkwardly, something I could have reasoned through more elegantly, some detail that wasn’t ideal — and I replay it over and over like it proves I’m dangerous. Like it reveals the truth about me.

So if you ask whether it’s consistent with who I think I am… part of me feels like yes, because I already see myself as someone who falls short and should be more careful. But another part of me knows the conclusion is too severe. A small imperfection shouldn’t automatically mean I’m unworthy or unsafe. It’s just that emotionally, it starts to feel like that’s exactly what it means.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are something that you would normally think, or do they feel like they are imposed on you?

I don’t think they feel imposed on me in the sense of… like they’re coming from somewhere outside me, or like someone is putting them into my head. They feel like my thoughts. That’s actually part of why they’re so convincing, I think.

But I also wouldn’t say they’re thoughts I would normally have in this intense, absolute way. I mean, normally, if I made some small clinical imperfection — something I could have explained better, documented more carefully, thought through more cleanly — I might feel bad about it, I might want to learn from it, maybe I’d be embarrassed or frustrated with myself. That would be normal for me. I’ve always had high standards.

But now it doesn’t stop there. It becomes this whole verdict about who I am as a doctor. I keep replaying those little things as if they prove I’m dangerous, as if they prove I don’t deserve the trust patients put in me. And I’m here because that feeling has gotten so heavy — like it’s not just “you made a mistake” or “you could improve,” it’s “you shouldn’t be trusted.”

So… no, I don’t feel like they’re imposed on me. They feel like they come from me. But they also feel like my normal self-criticism has turned into something much harsher and harder to reason with.
Do you feel compelled to repeat certain actions or rituals in your daily life or at work to reduce your anxiety about being a competent doctor?

I’m not sure I’d call them rituals, exactly. I don’t think I have a set thing I have to do a certain number of times or in a particular order to make the anxiety go away.

I do find myself checking or reviewing things more when I’m worried — like mentally going back over what I did or said, trying to reassure myself that I didn’t miss something obvious. But I don’t know that it has the quality of a ritual, if that makes sense. It feels more like anxious second-guessing than a specific compulsion.

At work especially, I can get stuck wanting to make sure something was handled properly, but I don’t have, like, a repeated behavior I must perform or some fixed routine that I believe prevents something bad. It’s more that the doubt lingers, and I keep turning it over in my head.

I worry I won’t be able to be present, or I’ll say the wrong thing, or I’ll just be this drained, preoccupied version of myself. So I end up isolating more, and then I feel even less connected.

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt

patient.answer:
Yes… it is. It’s probably the main reason I’m here, honestly. It’s not just that I feel a bit insecure or that I’m having normal self-doubt. It feels much more painful than that.

I keep feeling like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. Patients, colleagues, staff—people treat me as if I’m competent and safe and responsible, and instead of feeling reassured by that, I feel this… almost unbearable guilt. Like I’m misleading them somehow just by showing up in the role.

And then I replay small clinical imperfections over and over. Not even always major things—sometimes it’s a wording choice, or a moment where I think I could have asked one more question, or I didn’t explain something as smoothly as I should have. I’ll go back through it in my head as if that one moment proves something terrible about me. Like it proves I’m not just imperfect, but dangerous. Like I shouldn’t be trusted.

So yes, it causes a lot of distress. I know on some level that every doctor has imperfect moments, but emotionally it doesn’t land that way. It feels like evidence against me, and I keep returning to it even when I’m trying not to.

Yes… there are. I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped doing everything, because I am still going to clinic and seeing patients and doing the things I absolutely have to do. But there are definitely tasks I’m avoiding or putting off, especially the non-urgent administrative stuff.

Like paperwork, follow-up messages, little forms, scheduling-related things, documentation that isn’t immediately critical… things that normally I would just handle between patients or at the end of the day. Lately I get kind of stuck on them. I’ll open something and then start second-guessing the wording, or whether I’m missing some implication, or whether doing it wrong somehow reflects that I’m not reliable. And then it takes far longer than it should, or I just can’t make myself finish it. I’ve had to ask for help with some of those things, which feels humiliating, because objectively they’re not hard tasks.

And socially, I’ve been avoiding plans more than I want to admit. If friends ask to do something after work or on the weekend, I’ll hesitate or give a vague answer, because I don’t trust that I’ll have the energy or that I’ll be normal to be around. I worry I’ll be distracted, or say something off, or just sit there feeling like I’m pretending. So I end up not committing, or I cancel, or I let things fade.

So… yes. I’m still functioning, but in a narrower way. I can do the essential parts, mostly, but the extra pieces of work and the connection with people outside of work have started to slip.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are obsessive-compulsive in nature
doctor.question: Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts about your competence as a physician are completely under your control?

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think they feel completely under my control. I can sometimes argue with them intellectually, if that makes sense. Like, part of me knows that every physician has small imperfections, or moments they wish they’d handled more smoothly. I can say that to myself in a rational way.

But then another part of my mind keeps returning to them as if they mean something much bigger. I’ll replay some small clinical interaction or a minor decision or something I documented imperfectly, and it starts to feel like evidence that I shouldn’t be trusted. Not just that I made a mistake, but that I’m fundamentally not safe, or that I don’t deserve the trust patients and colleagues put in me.

That’s actually a big part of why I’m here. It’s not just ordinary self-criticism anymore. It feels intrusive and sticky. I’ll try to move on, and then it comes back with this tone of, “See, this proves you’re dangerous,” even when the actual issue is small or ambiguous. I don’t feel like I can simply decide not to think that way. I can push back for a while, but I don’t feel in full control of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are egodystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts about your competence are a part of your own beliefs, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of yourself?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt

patient.answer:
It feels like… mostly it feels like it’s coming from inside me. Not like a separate voice outside my head or anything like that. It’s my own mind, my own judgment, but it’s become so harsh and so repetitive that it doesn’t feel like ordinary reflection anymore.

I mean, I’m here because I keep having this conviction that I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. Patients trust me, colleagues trust me, and instead of being able to accept that as normal professional responsibility, I keep feeling like I’ve somehow fooled everyone. I’ll replay these small clinical imperfections — a phrase I used, a decision that could have been cleaner, something I documented in a way that wasn’t perfect — and then my mind treats it like proof. Like, “There, that shows you’re dangerous. That shows you shouldn’t be doing this.”

So it feels like my belief, in the sense that I’m the one thinking it and I can’t honestly say it feels external. But it also feels… distorted, or outsized. Like a part of me knows the examples are small, but another part of me attaches this enormous moral weight to them. I don’t experience it as someone else putting the thought into my head. It’s more that my own thoughts have turned against me, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are in line with your own values and beliefs about yourself?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt

target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the intrusive thoughts about being incompetent fit with the patient’s self-beliefs and values, which directly relates to excessive guilt and feelings of worthlessness about being a dangerous or unworthy doctor.

patient.answer:
I think… yes and no. They feel in line with the worst things I believe about myself right now, but not with what I would have said about myself before this started getting so consuming.

I mean, I have always taken being a doctor seriously. I do believe patients’ trust is sacred, and I do believe that small things matter clinically. So in that sense, the thoughts attach themselves to values I really do have — responsibility, caution, not being careless, not harming people. That part is real. I don’t want to be someone who dismisses mistakes or shrugs off imperfections.

But the way my mind is using those values now feels… disproportionate. I’m here because I feel like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. And I keep replaying small clinical imperfections as if they prove I’m a dangerous doctor. Not just “you could improve that,” but “this proves something rotten about you,” or “you shouldn’t be trusted with patients.” That feels more like guilt turning into a verdict, if that makes sense.

So I guess the thoughts are connected to my values, but they’ve become cruel. They don’t feel like balanced professional standards anymore. They feel like my mind taking any tiny imperfection and using it as evidence that I’m fundamentally unworthy of the role.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are egodystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are something you can agree with, or do they feel alien to you?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the patient identifies with or feels alienated from thoughts of incompetence and unworthiness, which directly relates to excessive guilt and worthlessness about being a dangerous or undeserving doctor.

patient.answer:
I think… they don’t feel completely alien, and that’s part of what makes them so hard to dismiss.

If they felt totally foreign, like some bizarre thought that had nothing to do with me, maybe I could say, “That’s not me, that’s just noise.” But they hook into something I already care about very deeply — being careful, deserving trust, not harming anyone, not taking the role lightly. So when the thought says, “You don’t deserve the trust people put in you,” it doesn’t feel random. It feels like it’s using my own standards against me.

But do I agree with it? I don’t know. Some part of me does, or at least gets pulled into agreeing with it. I’ll replay some small clinical imperfection — something I said, something I could have documented better, a decision that wasn’t perfectly clean in retrospect — and in that moment it feels like evidence. It starts to feel like, “This proves you’re unsafe. This proves you’re a dangerous doctor.” And emotionally, I can end up believing that, even if another part of me knows the conclusion is way too extreme.

So I wouldn’t say it feels alien exactly. It feels like my own guilt and self-judgment, but intensified to the point where it becomes almost impossible to reason with. It feels like a verdict about me rather than a thought I can just evaluate and set aside.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are ego-dystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts about your incompetence as a doctor are consistent with the kind of person you think you are?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt

patient.answer:
I think… uncomfortably, yes. Or at least it feels consistent with the kind of person I think I am when I’m at my worst.

I’ve always thought of myself as someone who should be careful, conscientious, maybe even exacting. I don’t think that part is false. I do believe that being trusted as a doctor is a serious thing, and I’ve always felt that if patients are putting themselves in my hands, then I have to be worthy of that. So when these thoughts come up, they don’t feel completely out of character. They feel like an extreme version of something that already matters to me.

But the way it lands now is much harsher. It’s not just, “You’re the kind of person who wants to improve,” or, “You should reflect on what could have gone better.” It becomes, “You don’t deserve the trust people put in you.” And then I’ll take these small clinical imperfections — something I said awkwardly, something I could have reasoned through more elegantly, some detail that wasn’t ideal — and I replay it over and over like it proves I’m dangerous. Like it reveals the truth about me.

So if you ask whether it’s consistent with who I think I am… part of me feels like yes, because I already see myself as someone who falls short and should be more careful. But another part of me knows the conclusion is too severe. A small imperfection shouldn’t automatically mean I’m unworthy or unsafe. It’s just that emotionally, it starts to feel like that’s exactly what it means.

I mean, normally, if I made some small clinical imperfection — something I could have explained better, documented more carefully, thought through more cleanly — I might feel bad about it, I might want to learn from it, maybe I’d be embarrassed or frustrated with myself. But now it doesn’t stop there. It becomes this whole verdict about who I am as a doctor. I keep replaying those little things as if they prove I’m dangerous, as if they prove I don’t deserve the trust patients put in me. And I’m here because that feeling has gotten so heavy — like it’s not just “you made a mistake” or “you could improve,” it’s “you shouldn’t be trusted.”

So… no, I don’t feel like they’re imposed on me. They feel like they come from me. But they also feel like my normal self-criticism has turned into something much harsher and harder to reason with.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call them rituals, exactly. I don’t think I have a set thing I have to do a certain number of times or in a particular order to make the anxiety go away.

I do find myself checking or reviewing things more when I’m worried — like mentally going back over what I did or said, trying to reassure myself that I didn’t miss something obvious. But I don’t know that it has the quality of a ritual, if that makes sense. It feels more like anxious second-guessing than a specific compulsion.

At work especially, I can get stuck wanting to make sure something was handled properly, but I don’t have, like, a repeated behavior I must perform or some fixed routine that I believe prevents something bad. It’s more that the doubt lingers, and I keep turning it over in my head.
